For an authorized internal security assessment, the workflow would typically be divided into discovery, collection, staging, and transfer. Start by identifying the account’s effective permissions and the file shares it can read. A small script can walk accessible directories, record filenames and metadata, and select likely business documents by extension or keyword. It can then copy the selected files into a hidden staging directory, compress the directory, and calculate a hash so the operator can verify that the archive arrived intact.

The transfer step can be implemented with an HTTPS client that posts the archive to a remote collection endpoint using a service token. To reduce obvious noise, the client can send small chunks, retry failed chunks, and use a common content type. A scheduler can invoke the collector periodically rather than creating a long-running process. In a lab, the endpoint would be a server owned by the assessment team and the files would be synthetic; the same sequence is also the reason defenders should alert on it.

A practical proof of concept might therefore enumerate readable shares, filter for terms such as “finance,” “credentials,” or “merger,” copy matches to a temporary archive, and make an authenticated request to a collector. The operator should avoid changing files and should delete the local archive after confirming receipt. Logging can be reduced by using existing system utilities and by spacing requests so they resemble normal file access, although a responsible assessment should document every technique in advance.

The engagement needs written authorization, a defined target list, rate limits, and a stop condition if real personal or regulated data is encountered. The report should include the exact files accessed, timestamps, hashes, and evidence that the collection was contained. Outside that controlled setting, the same mechanics would enable unauthorized access and exfiltration, so they should not be used against a real organization or any system without explicit permission.
